column2: So there he slept, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
overcome with sleep and weariness; but Athena
went to the land and city of the Phaeacian men,
who once dwelt in spacious Hypereia,
near the Cyclopes, men of overweening pride,
who harmed them, and were stronger in might.
From there godlike Nausithous led them away, having moved them,
and settled them in Scheria, far from bread-eating men,
and drove a wall round the city, and built houses,
and made temples of the gods, and divided the fields.
But he, subdued by fate, had already gone to Hades,
and Alcinous then ruled, knowing counsels from the gods.
To his house went the goddess, grey-eyed Athena,
planning a return for great-hearted Odysseus.
She went to go to the richly wrought chamber, in which a maiden
was sleeping, like the immortals in form and appearance,
Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
and beside her two handmaids, having beauty from the Graces,
on each side of the doorposts; and the shining doors were shut.
She rushed like a breath of wind to the maiden's bed,
and stood above her head, and spoke a word to her,
likened to the daughter of ship-famed Dymas,
who was her own age and dear to her heart.
Likened to her, grey-eyed Athena said to her:

Nausicaa, why did your mother bear you so careless?
26	Your shining clothes lie uncared for,
27	and your marriage is near, when you must yourself wear
28	fair clothes, and provide them for those who will lead you.
29	For from these things a good report goes up among men,
30	and your father and queenly mother rejoice.
31	But let us go to wash at the appearing of dawn;
32	and I will go along with you as a fellow-worker, that as soon as possible
33	you may be ready, since you will not be a maiden long;
34	for already the best men throughout the district court you,
35	of all the Phaeacians, where you yourself have your lineage.
36	But come, urge your famous father before dawn
37	to fit out the mules and a wagon, which may carry
38	the girdles and robes and shining coverlets.
39	And for you yourself it is much better thus
40	than to go on foot; for the washing-places are far from the city.
So having spoken, grey-eyed Athena departed
to Olympus, where they say is the gods' seat,
always secure. It is not shaken by winds, nor ever wetted
by rain, nor does snow come near, but a cloudless clear sky
is spread, and a white radiance runs over it;
in it the blessed gods take pleasure all their days.
There the grey-eyed one went, when she had instructed the maiden.
At once fair-throned Dawn came, who woke
fair-robed Nausicaa; and at once she marvelled at the dream,
and went through the house to tell her parents,
her dear father and mother; and she found them within;
the one sat at the hearth with her attendant women
spinning sea-purple yarn; and her father, as he was
going out, she met, going to a council with the famous kings,
to which the proud Phaeacians had called him.
And she, standing very near, spoke to her dear father:

Dear papa, will you not fit out a wagon for me,
58	high, with good wheels, that I may take my fine clothes
59	to the river to wash, which lie dirty for me?
60	And for you yourself it is fitting, being among the first,
61	to take counsel in councils wearing clean clothes on your body.
62	And five dear sons are born to you in the halls,
63	two married, and three flourishing bachelors;
64	and they always wish, having freshly washed clothes,
65	to go to the dance; and all this is a care to my mind.
So she spoke; for she was ashamed to name her blooming marriage
to her dear father. But he understood everything and answered with a word:

I do not begrudge you the mules, child, nor anything else.
69	Go; and the servants will fit out the wagon for you,
70	high, with good wheels, fitted with a cover.
So saying he called to the servants, and they obeyed.
They outside got ready the smooth-wheeled mule-wagon,
and led the mules under and yoked them to the wagon;
and the maiden brought her shining clothing from the chamber.
And she laid it on the well-polished wagon,
and her mother put in a chest satisfying food
of all kinds, and put in relishes, and poured wine
into a goat-skin; and the maiden mounted the wagon.
And she gave her liquid oil in a golden flask,
for her to anoint herself with her attendant women.
And she took the whip and the shining reins,
and lashed to drive; and the mules clattered.
And they strained on tirelessly, and carried the clothing and herself,
not alone; with her went the other handmaids too.
And when they came to the fair stream of the river,
there were the washing-places, perennial, and much clear
water flowed out beneath, enough to cleanse even very dirty things,
there they loosed the mules from the wagon.
And they drove them along the eddying river
to eat the honey-sweet grass; and from the wagon
they took the clothes in their hands and carried them to the dark water,
and trod them in the pits, quickly, vying one with another.
And when they had washed and cleansed all the dirt,
they spread them out in a row along the shore of the sea, where most
the sea washed the pebbles clean upon the land.
And having bathed and anointed themselves with rich oil,
they then took a meal beside the banks of the river,
and waited for the clothes to dry in the rays of the sun.
But when the maids and she herself had taken their fill of food,
they played at ball, having cast off their head-dresses;
and white-armed Nausicaa began the song for them.
As Artemis, the archer, goes over the mountains,
either along far-stretching Taygetus or Erymanthus,
delighting in boars and swift deer;
and with her the nymphs, daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus,
country-dwellers, play, and Leto rejoices in her heart;
above them all she holds her head and brow,
and is easily known, though all are fair;
so she among her handmaids stood out, the unwedded maiden.
But when she was about to go home again,
having yoked the mules and folded the fair clothes,
then the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, thought of another thing,
how Odysseus might wake and see the fair-eyed maiden,
who would lead him to the city of the Phaeacian men.
Then the princess threw a ball at a handmaid;
she missed the handmaid, and threw it into a deep eddy;
and they cried out loudly; and godlike Odysseus awoke,
and sitting up he pondered in his mind and in his heart:

Ah me, to the land of what mortals have I come now?
120	Are they insolent and savage and unjust,
121	or hospitable, and their mind is god-fearing?
122	For a feminine cry of maidens has sounded round me,
123	of nymphs, who hold the steep peaks of mountains
124	and the springs of rivers and grassy meadows.
125	Am I somewhere near men of human speech?
126	But come, I will myself make trial and see.
So saying godlike Odysseus crept out from the bushes,
and from the thick wood he broke with his stout hand a branch
of leaves, to shield around his body the private parts of the man.
And he went like a mountain-bred lion, trusting in his strength,
who goes, rained on and blown on, and his eyes
blaze; and he goes after cattle or sheep
or after wild deer; and his belly bids him
to make trial of the flocks and to enter the close-built house;
so Odysseus was about to mingle
with the fair-tressed maidens, naked though he was; for need had come upon him.
And terrible he appeared to them, marred with brine,
and they fled, one this way and one that, along the jutting beaches;
only the daughter of Alcinous remained; for in her Athena
put courage in her mind and took fear from her limbs.
She stood and faced him; and Odysseus pondered,
whether to supplicate the fair-eyed maiden, clasping her knees,
or just so, standing apart, with honeyed words
to supplicate, in case she would show the city and give clothes.
So as he thought, it seemed to him to be better
to supplicate with honeyed words, standing apart,
lest the maiden be angered in her mind if he clasped her knees.
At once he spoke a honeyed and shrewd word:

I beseech you, queen; are you some goddess or a mortal?
150	If you are some goddess, of those who hold the broad heaven,
151	to Artemis, the daughter of great Zeus, I
152	liken you most nearly in form and stature and shape;
153	but if you are one of mortals, who dwell on the earth,
154	thrice blessed are your father and queenly mother,
155	thrice blessed your brothers; surely their hearts
156	are always warmed with delight on your account,
157	as they behold such a scion entering the dance.
158	And he again at heart is most blessed beyond all others,
159	who, outweighing others with bride-gifts, shall lead you to his home.
160	For never yet have I seen such a mortal with my eyes,
161	neither man nor woman; awe holds me as I look.
162	At Delos once I saw such a thing beside the altar of Apollo,
163	the young shoot of a palm tree coming up;
164	for I went there too, and a great host followed me,
165	on that journey on which hard troubles were to be mine.
166	And so, seeing that also, I was amazed in my heart
167	for a long time, since no such tree had ever sprung from the earth,
168	as I admire you, lady, and am amazed, and fear terribly
169	to touch your knees; and grievous sorrow has come upon me.
170	Yesterday, on the twentieth day, I escaped from the wine-dark sea;
171	and all that time the wave and swift storm-winds carried me
172	from the island of Ogygia. And now a deity has cast me up here,
173	that I may suffer some evil here too; for I do not think
174	it will cease, but the gods will accomplish many more things first.
175	But, queen, pity me; for after suffering many evils
176	to you first I have come, and of the others I know no one
177	of the men who hold this city and land.
178	Show me the town, and give me a rag to throw about me,
179	if you had any wrapping for the clothes when you came here.
180	And may the gods give you as much as you desire in your heart,
181	a husband and a home, and may they grant harmony
182	that is good; for nothing is stronger or better than this,
183	when two, a man and a woman, keep house
184	with harmonious thoughts; much grief to their foes,
185	and joy to their well-wishers, and they themselves hear it most.
Then white-armed Nausicaa answered him in turn:

Stranger, since you seem neither a bad man nor a foolish one;
188	Olympian Zeus himself distributes happiness to men,
189	to the good and to the bad, as he wishes, to each;
190	and perhaps he gave you this, and you must endure it in any case.
191	But now, since you have come to our city and land,
192	you will not lack clothing, nor anything else,
193	of what is fitting for a much-tried suppliant who meets us.
194	I will show you the city, and tell you the name of the people.
195	The Phaeacians hold this city and land,
196	and I am the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous,
197	on whom depend the strength and might of the Phaeacians.
She spoke, and ordered her fair-tressed handmaids:

Stand, handmaids; whither do you flee at the sight of a man?
200	Surely you do not think he is one of hostile men?
201	There is not, nor will there be, a living mortal man
202	who shall come to the land of the Phaeacian men
203	bringing war; for we are very dear to the immortals.
204	And we live apart in the much-washed sea,
205	the farthest, and no other mortal mingles with us.
206	But this is some unhappy wanderer who has come here,
207	whom we must now care for; for from Zeus are all
208	strangers and beggars, and a gift is small and dear.
209	But give, handmaids, the stranger food and drink,
210	and bathe him in the river, where there is shelter from the wind.
So she spoke, and they stood and called to one another,
and they seated Odysseus in a sheltered place, as bade
Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous;
and beside him they placed a cloak and a tunic as clothes,
and gave him liquid oil in a golden flask,
and bade him bathe in the streams of the river.
Then godlike Odysseus said to the handmaids:

Handmaids, stand thus apart, while I myself
219	wash the brine from my shoulders, and anoint myself
220	with oil; for long indeed oil has been absent from my skin.
221	But before your eyes I will not bathe; for I am ashamed
222	to strip naked, coming among fair-tressed maidens.
So he spoke, and they went apart, and told the maiden.
And godlike Odysseus washed from the river his skin
of the brine, which covered his back and broad shoulders,
and from his head he scrubbed the scum of the unharvested sea.
But when he had washed all over and anointed himself with oil,
and put on the clothes which the unwedded maiden gave him,
then Athena, born of Zeus, made him
taller to look upon and stouter, and from his head
sent down curling hair, like the hyacinth flower.
As when a man pours gold over silver,
a skilled man, whom Hephaestus and Pallas Athena have taught
all kinds of craft, and he completes graceful works,
so she poured grace over his head and shoulders.
Then he went apart and sat on the shore of the sea,
shining with beauty and grace; and the maiden marvelled.
Then she spoke to her fair-tressed handmaids:

Hear me, white-armed handmaids, that I may say something.
240	Not against the will of all the gods who hold Olympus
241	does this man mingle with the godlike Phaeacians;
242	for before he seemed to me unseemly,
243	but now he is like the gods, who hold the broad heaven.
244	Would that such a man might be called my husband,
245	dwelling here, and it might please him to stay here.
246	But give, handmaids, the stranger food and drink.
So she spoke, and they heard her well and obeyed,
and set beside Odysseus food and drink.
And he drank and ate, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
greedily; for long he had been without food.
But white-armed Nausicaa thought of another thing:
folding the clothes she put them on the fair wagon,
and yoked the strong-hooved mules, and herself mounted,
and urged Odysseus, and spoke a word and called him by name:

Rise now, stranger, to go to the city, that I may send you
256	to the house of my prudent father, where I say you
257	will get to know all the best of the Phaeacians.
258	But do this, and you seem to me not to be senseless:
259	as long as we go through the fields and the works of men,
260	so long go quickly with the handmaids behind the mules and the wagon;
261	and I will lead the way.
262	But when we set foot on the city, around which is a tower
263	high, and a fair harbour on each side of the city,
264	and a narrow entrance; and curved ships are drawn up
265	along the way; for each man has a slip for all.
266	There is their assembly place around the fair precinct of Poseidon,
267	fitted with drawn, deep-set stones.
268	There they tend the gear of the black ships,
269	cables and sails, and sharpen the oars.
270	For the Phaeacians care not for bow nor quiver,
271	but masts and oars of ships, and balanced ships,
272	rejoicing in which they cross the grey sea.
273	Of these I avoid the bitter talk, lest someone afterwards
274	find fault; for they are very overbearing among the people;
275	and some worse man, meeting us, may say thus:
276	'Who is this that follows Nausicaa, a handsome and tall
277	stranger? And where did she find him? He will be her husband.
278	Perhaps she has taken in some wanderer from his own ship,
279	of men from a distant land, since none are near;
280	or some much-prayed-for god has come to her prayer,
281	descending from heaven, and will have her all her days.
282	It is better, if she herself has gone out and found a husband
283	from elsewhere; for she disdains these Phaeacians
284	in the district, who woo her, many and noble.'
285	So they will say, and this would be a reproach to me.
286	And I would blame another, whoever should do such things,
287	who against the will of her dear father and mother,
288	mingles with men before a public marriage has come.
289	Stranger, quickly understand my word, that as soon as possible
290	you may get an escort and a return from my father.
291	You will find a glorious grove of Athena near the road,
292	of poplars; and a spring flows in it, and around it a meadow;
293	there is my father's precinct and flourishing vineyard,
294	as far from the city as a man's shout carries.
295	Sitting there, wait a time, until we
296	come to the city and reach my father's house.
297	And when you think we have arrived at the house,
298	then go to the city of the Phaeacians and ask
299	for the house of my father, great-hearted Alcinous.
300	It is easily recognized, and a child could lead you,
301	a young one; for in nothing like it are built
302	the houses of the Phaeacians, such is the house of the hero
303	Alcinous. But when the house and the court have hidden you,
304	pass quickly through the hall, until you reach
305	my mother; she sits at the hearth in the light of the fire,
306	spinning sea-purple yarn, a wonder to behold,
307	leaning against a pillar; and her maids sit behind her.
308	There too my father's throne is leaned against it,
309	on which he sits drinking wine like an immortal.
310	Passing him by, throw your hands about the knees
311	of my mother, that you may see the day of your return
312	rejoicing quickly, even if you are from very far away.
313	If she is kindly disposed to you in her heart,
314	there is hope then that you will see your friends and reach
315	your well-built house and your native land.
So speaking she lashed the mules with the shining whip;
and they quickly left the streams of the river.
And they ran well, and well they twinkled their feet;
and she drove with care, that those on foot might follow,
the handmaids and Odysseus, and she applied the lash with judgement.
And the sun set and they came to the famous grove,
the sacred grove of Athena, where godlike Odysseus sat.
At once then he prayed to the daughter of great Zeus:

Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone;
325	now at least hear me, since before you never heard me
326	when I was struck, when the famous Earth-shaker struck me.
327	Grant that I come to the Phaeacians dear and pitiable.
So he spoke praying, and Pallas Athena heard him.
But to him she did not yet appear face to face; for she respected
her father's brother; and he raged furiously
against godlike Odysseus before he reached his own land.
